figures.cap: right-angled triangle ABT with right angle at B, angle 26 degrees at A, height h

parts.latex:
A tower $BT$ has height $h$ metres.

From point $A$, the angle of elevation to the top of the tower is $26^\circ$ as shown.

\exfigure{268_q3_1}

Which of the following is the correct expression for the length of $AB$?

solutions.latex:
In right-angled triangle $ABT$, $BT$ is opposite the $26^\circ$ angle and $AB$ is adjacent:
$$\begin{aligned} \tan 26^\circ &= \dfrac{h}{AB} \\ AB &= \dfrac{h}{\tan 26^\circ} \\ &= h\cot 26^\circ \end{aligned}$$

613.stem:
A helicopter leaves Underwood and flies 70 km on a bearing of $055^\circ$ to Vacy.

It then flies 82 km on a bearing of $150^\circ$ to Woodville.

The diagram below illustrates the journey.

\exfigure{1369_q19_1}

figures.cap: bearings diagram U, V, W
solution sketch: bearings diagram with 55 and 30 degree angles and theta at W

parts.latex:
The helicopter then plans to fly directly to Underwood.

Calculate, to the nearest km, the distance that it will fly.

Determine the bearing (from Woodville) on which it should fly to return to Underwood.

Give your answer to the nearest degree.

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{1369_q19_s1}

$\angle UVW=55^\circ+30^\circ=85^\circ$ (co-interior angles with the north lines).

By the cosine rule in $\triangle UVW$:
$$\begin{aligned}UW^2&=70^2+82^2-2\times 70\times 82\cos 85^\circ\\ &=10623.45\ldots\\ UW&=103.07\ldots\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ It will fly $103$ km (nearest km).
criteria: Correct use of cosine rule, or equivalent merit

meta.concern: transcribed from handwritten solutions on scanned pages (no text layer); marking guideline gives no mark criteria; criteria written to house style
meta.top_criterion_original:
Correct answer
1: Correct use of cosine rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Let $\angle UWV=\theta$. By the cosine rule:
$$\begin{aligned}\cos\theta&=\dfrac{103^2+82^2-70^2}{2\times 103\times 82}\\ &=0.736\ldots\\ \theta&=42.605\ldots^\circ\\ &\approx 43^\circ\ \text{(nearest degree)}\end{aligned}$$
The bearing of $V$ from $W$ is $360^\circ-30^\circ$, and $U$ is a further $43^\circ$ anticlockwise, so the bearing from $W$ to $U$ is
$$360^\circ-30^\circ-43^\circ=287^\circ\text{T}$$

Cosine rule.evidence: Finds ∠WLC using the cosine rule or the sine rule
Cosine rule.reason: Criterion accepts cosine rule or sine rule: free choice of method.

Sine rule.evidence: Finds ∠WLC using the cosine rule or the sine rule
Sine rule.reason: Criterion accepts cosine rule or sine rule: free choice of method.

solutions.latex: \exfigure{1356_q22_s1}

The bearing of $L$ from $W$ is $258^\circ$, so measured anticlockwise from north:
$$\begin{aligned}\angle NWL+258^\circ&=360^\circ\\\angle NWL&=102^\circ\end{aligned}$$
The bearing of $C$ from $W$ is $280^\circ$, so $\angle NWC=80^\circ$:
$$\begin{aligned}\angle CWL&=102^\circ-80^\circ\\&=22^\circ\end{aligned}$$
Using the cosine rule in $\triangle CWL$, $c^2=a^2+b^2-2ab\cos C$:
$$\begin{aligned}CL^2&=10^2+6^2-2\times 10\times 6\cos 22^\circ\\&=24.73793745\\CL&=4.973724706\\&\approx 4.97\text{ km}\ (2\text{ decimal places})\end{aligned}$$

Using the cosine rule in $\triangle CWL$ to find $\angle WLC$:
$$\begin{aligned}\cos\angle WLC&=\dfrac{CL^2+WL^2-CW^2}{2\times CL\times WL}\\&=\dfrac{4.97\ldots^2+6^2-10^2}{2\times 4.97\ldots\times 6}\\&=-0.6578246162\\\angle WLC&=131.1341759^\circ\\&\approx 131^\circ\end{aligned}$$
$\angle NWL=102^\circ$ (part (b)), and the north lines at $W$ and $L$ are parallel:
$$\begin{aligned}\angle WLN&=180^\circ-102^\circ\\&=78^\circ\quad(\text{co-interior angles})\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\angle NLC&=131^\circ-78^\circ\\&=53^\circ\end{aligned}$$
$C$ is $53^\circ$ anticlockwise from north at $L$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Bearing}&=360^\circ-53^\circ\\&=307^\circ T\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds $\angle WLC$ using the cosine rule or the sine rule, or equivalent merit
Finds an expression for $\cos\angle WLC$ or $\sin\angle WLC$, or equivalent merit

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the angle $131^\circ-78^\circ=53^\circ$ was labelled $\angle NWL$; it is $\angle NLC$ (at $L$).

708.stem:
Sally is training for the swim leg of a triathlon and decides to go for a training swim in the harbour. She starts at a jetty $J$ and swims on a bearing of $105^\circ$ for 5 km out to a buoy $L$. She then changes direction and swims on a bearing of $045^\circ$ for a further 16 km to buoy $M$.

\exfigure{1363_q23_1}

figures.cap: bearings diagram: J to L 5 km on 105 degrees, L to M 16 km on 045 degrees; NOT TO SCALE

parts.latex: Find $\angle JLM$.
Find the distance $JM$ that Sally will swim back to the jetty.
Find the bearing of jetty $J$ from the buoy $L$.

solutions.latex:
The north lines at $J$ and $L$ are parallel, so the angle between $LJ$ and north at $L$ is $180^\circ-105^\circ=75^\circ$ (co-interior angles). $LM$ is $45^\circ$ on the other side of north:
$$\begin{aligned} \angle JLM&=75^\circ+45^\circ\\ &=120^\circ \end{aligned}$$

Cosine rule in $\triangle JLM$:
$$\begin{aligned} JM^2&=5^2+16^2-2\times5\times16\times\cos 120^\circ\\ &=361\\ JM&=19\text{ km} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Applies the cosine rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
From (a), $LJ$ is $75^\circ$ anticlockwise from north at $L$; bearings are measured clockwise from north:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Bearing}&=360^\circ-75^\circ\\ &=285^\circ \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
At 9 am, Brooklyn is 11 km due north of camp, while Milan is 12 km due east of camp. Their positions are shown on the diagram below.

\exfigure{1357_q14_1}

They both start walking directly towards camp at a speed of 4 kilometres per hour.

Find the distance between Brooklyn and Milan at 11 am.

solutions.latex:
In 2 hours each walks $2 \times 4 = 8$ km towards camp.

At 11 am Brooklyn is $11 - 8 = 3$ km from camp and Milan is $12 - 8 = 4$ km from camp.

By Pythagoras' theorem (north and east are at right angles):
$$\begin{aligned} d &= \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} \\ &= 5 \text{ km} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct use of Pythagoras' theorem with the new distances, or equivalent merit

figures.cap: Wheel with centre O touching the track at M, arrow showing direction of rolling
solution sketch: Wheel after rolling, M' above the track with right triangle at O, height h

parts.latex: Through what angle does $M$ rotate about $O$ (in radians) after the wheel rolls 1 metre ?
After the wheel rolls 1 metre, what is the vertical height of $M$ above the track? (answer to the nearest cm)

Arc length.evidence: The angle in the right-angled triangle is 5/2−π/2
Arc length.reason: Rolling 1 m gives θ=100/40=5/2 rad via l=rθ.

solutions.latex:
Using the arc length formula $l=r\theta$, with $l=100$ cm and $r=40$ cm:
$$\begin{aligned} 100 &= 40\theta \\ \theta &= \dfrac{5}{2} \text{ radians} \end{aligned}$$

\exfigure{377_q18_s1}

$M'$ is where $M$ rolls to, and $h$ is the height of $M'$ above the track.

The angle in the right-angled triangle is $\dfrac{5}{2}-\dfrac{\pi}{2}=\dfrac{5-\pi}{2}$ radians.

In this triangle, $\sin\dfrac{5-\pi}{2}=\dfrac{x}{40}$, so
$$x=40\sin\dfrac{5-\pi}{2}$$
$$\begin{aligned} h &= 40+x \\ &= 40+40\sin\left(\dfrac{5-\pi}{2}\right) \\ &\approx 72.0457 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ h=72 \text{ cm (nearest cm)}$$
criteria: Finds the correct expression for $x$, or equivalent merit
Finds the correct angle in the triangle, or equivalent merit

The bird is $h-1.6$ metres above Kelly's eyes. The angle of depression of Kelly from the bird is $73^\circ$, so by alternate angles the angle of elevation of the bird from Kelly's eyes is $73^\circ$.

2517.stem:
There are three towns in a rural area. Town $B$ is 37 km from Town $A$ at a bearing of $040^\circ$T. Town $C$ is 45 km from Town $B$ at a bearing of $160^\circ$T.

\exfigure{1614_q13_2}

figures.cap: bearings diagram of towns A, B, C

parts.latex: Find the size of $\angle ABC$.
Find the distance from Town $A$ to Town $C$, correct to 1 decimal place.
Find the bearing of Town $A$ from Town $C$.

solutions.latex: $$\angle ABC=40^\circ+20^\circ=60^\circ$$

meta.format_note: Working in source is brief; diagram not checked. Source check: Source gives 40°+20°=60°. With bearings 040° at B (from A) and 160° from B, the angle at B would be 180°−40°−(180°−160°)... check: ∠ABC = 40°+(180°−160°)=60° gives same answer, so source working is consistent but unexplained.

solutions.latex:
By the cosine rule in $\triangle ABC$, with $AB=37$, $BC=45$ and $\angle ABC=60^\circ$:
$$\begin{aligned} AC^2 &= 37^2+45^2-2\times37\times45\times\cos60^\circ \\ &= 1729 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} AC &= \sqrt{1729} \\ &= 41.5812\ldots \\ &\approx 41.6 \text{ km} \end{aligned}$$
The distance from $A$ to $C$ is $41.6$ km (no penalty for incorrect rounding).
criteria: Correct cosine rule substitution, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Diagram of the triangle not added.

solutions.latex:
By the cosine rule in $\triangle ABC$, find $\angle BAC$:
$$\cos\angle BAC=\dfrac{37^2+1729-45^2}{2\times37\times\sqrt{1729}}$$
so $\angle BAC=70^\circ$ (nearest degree; no penalty for using $41.6$ km).

The bearing of $C$ from $A$ is $110^\circ$T.

The bearing of $A$ from $C$ is the reverse bearing:
$$110^\circ+180^\circ=290^\circ\text{T}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the bearing of } A \text{ from } C \text{ is } 290^\circ\text{T}$$
criteria: Correct $\angle BAC$ (or bearing of $A$ to $C$ identified), or equivalent merit

figures.cap: points P, Q, R with bearing 070 and distances 16 km and 35 km

parts.latex: Find the distance of $R$ from $Q$. Answer correct to 1 decimal place.
Find the bearing of $R$ from $Q$. Answer correct to the nearest degree.

solutions.latex:
The bearing $070^\circ$ gives
$$\angle RPQ=90^\circ-70^\circ=20^\circ$$
Using the cosine rule in $\triangle PQR$:
$$\begin{aligned} RQ^{2}&=16^{2}+35^{2}-2\times16\times35\times\cos 20^\circ \\ &=428.54\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$$RQ=20.7\text{ km}$$
criteria: Applies the cosine rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Let $\angle RQP=\theta$. By the sine rule:
$$\dfrac{\sin\theta}{16}=\dfrac{\sin 20^\circ}{20.7}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \sin\theta&=\dfrac{16\sin 20^\circ}{20.7} \\ \theta&=\sin^{-1}(0.264) \\ &=15.3^\circ \end{aligned}$$
The obtuse value $180^\circ-15.3^\circ=164.7^\circ$ would make the angle sum of $\triangle PQR$ exceed $180^\circ$, so $\theta$ is acute.

Alternatively, by the cosine rule:
$$\begin{aligned} \cos\theta&=\dfrac{20.7^{2}+35^{2}-16^{2}}{2\times20.7\times35} \\ &=0.9645 \end{aligned}$$
So $\theta=15.30^\circ$.

The bearing is
$$270^\circ+15^\circ=285^\circ$$ to the nearest degree.
criteria: Uses the sine or cosine rule correctly to find $\theta$, or equivalent merit

2838.stem:
Manavdeep leaves island $A$ in a boat and sails 164 km on a bearing of $070^\circ$ to island $B$. He then sails on a bearing of $194^\circ$ for 241 km to island $C$, as shown in the diagram.

\exfigure{1322_q22_1}

figures.cap: bearings diagram, islands A, B, C
solution diagram (drawn by Claude)

parts.latex: Show that the size of $\angle ABC=56^\circ$.
Show that the distance from island $C$ to island $A$ is approximately $202\ \text{km}$.
Manavdeep wants to sail from island $C$ directly to island $A$. On what bearing should he sail? Give your answer to the nearest degree.

meta.format_note: Solution diagram requested by style: figure 1322_q22_s1 should be the question's diagram showing north lines at A and B, bearings 070° and 194°, AB = 164 km, BC = 241 km and angle ABC = 56°.

solutions.latex:
Using the cosine rule in triangle $ABC$:
$$AC^2=164^2+241^2-2\times164\times241\times\cos56^\circ$$
$$\begin{aligned} AC&=\sqrt{164^2+241^2-2\times164\times241\times\cos56^\circ} \\ &=201.9255\dots \\ &\approx202\ \text{km} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct use of the cosine rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the sine rule in triangle $ABC$:
$$\dfrac{\sin\angle ACB}{164}=\dfrac{\sin56^\circ}{202}$$
$$\sin\angle ACB=\dfrac{\sin56^\circ}{202}\times164$$
$$\angle ACB=42.305\dots\approx42^\circ\text{ (nearest degree)}$$
The bearing from $C$ to $A$ is
$$\begin{aligned} 360^\circ-\big[42^\circ-(194^\circ-180^\circ)\big]&=332^\circ \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the correct value of $\angle ACB$, or equivalent merit

3040.stem:
A horizontal bridge is built between points $A$ and $B$. The bridge is supported by cables $SP$ and $SR$, which are attached to the top of a vertical pylon $ST$.

\exfigure{1326_q14_1}

The section of the pylon, $SQ$, above the bridge is 8 metres long and $\angle SRQ=52^\circ$.

The distance $AQ$ is 22 metres, and $P$ is the midpoint of $AQ$

figures.cap: bridge, pylon SQ and cables SP, SR

parts.latex: Find the length of the cable $SR$.
Find the size of $\angle SPQ$ to the nearest degree.

solutions.latex:
In right-angled triangle $SQR$, $\sin52^\circ=\dfrac{SQ}{SR}$.
$$\begin{aligned} SR&=\dfrac{8}{\sin52^\circ} \\ &\approx10.15\text{ m} \end{aligned}$$

$P$ is the midpoint of $AQ$ and $AQ=22$ m, so $PQ=11$ m.

In right-angled triangle $SPQ$, $\tan\angle SPQ=\dfrac{SQ}{PQ}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \tan\angle SPQ&=\dfrac{8}{11} \\ \angle SPQ&=\tan^{-1}\dfrac{8}{11} \\ &\approx36^\circ \end{aligned}$$
to the nearest degree.
criteria: Recognises the tangent ratio but applies incorrect values, or equivalent merit

3087.stem:
A hiker walks 5 km from camp to point A in a direction of $N37^\circ W$. They then walk 3 km due west to point B, as shown in the diagram below.

\exfigure{1327_q27_1}

figures.cap: hiker path camp to A to B

parts.latex:
What is the shortest distance between the hiker when at point B and the camp?

(Answer to the nearest metre)

What is the bearing of the hiker at point B from the camp?

(Answer to the nearest degree)

solutions.latex:
In triangle camp-A-B, the angle at A is $\angle CAB = 127^\circ$. Use the cosine rule.
$$\begin{aligned} a^2 &= 3^2 + 5^2 - 2(3)(5)\cos 127^\circ \\ &= 52.05445\ldots \\ a &\approx 7.2149 \text{ km} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the distance is } 7215 \text{ m to the nearest metre}$$
criteria: Substitutes correctly into the cosine rule, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Diagram would help (bearings and triangle): sketch not added here, no sketch id for it. Rubric written by us. The source gives $\angle CAB=127^\circ$ without derivation (180° − 37° − ... not shown).

solutions.latex:
Let $\theta$ be the angle at the camp in the triangle. Use the sine rule.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\sin\theta}{3} &= \dfrac{\sin 127^\circ}{7.215} \\ \sin\theta &= \dfrac{3\sin 127^\circ}{7.215} \\ \theta &\approx 19.4^\circ \approx 19^\circ \end{aligned}$$
B is further west than A, so the bearing is
$$\begin{aligned} 360^\circ - (37^\circ + 19^\circ) &= 304^\circ \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{bearing } 304^\circ \text{ (or N}56^\circ\text{W)}$$

3822.stem:
A support cable, 80 metres long, has been secured at an angle of elevation of $60^\circ$ from point $A$ to the top of a building. A second support cable will be secured from point $B$, 20 metres closer to the base of the building than point $A$. This information is shown in the diagram.

\exfigure{1547_q12_1}

figures.cap: right triangle with cables from A and B to top of building

parts.latex: Show that the length of the second cable is approximately 72 metres.
Given that the height of the building is 69.2 metres, calculate the distance between point $A$ and the base of the building.

solutions.latex:
Let the second cable have length $c$. In the triangle formed by the two cables, the angle between the 80 m cable and the 20 m side at $A$ is $60^\circ$, so apply the cosine rule.
$$\begin{aligned} c^2&=20^2+80^2-2\times 20\times 80\cos 60^\circ\\ &=5200\\ c&=\sqrt{5200}\\ &=72.11102551\ldots\\ &\approx 72 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct use of the cosine rule, showing all steps to the approximated answer
Correct substitution into the cosine rule with a small calculation error, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Let $O$ be the base of the building.

Method 1 (right-angled trigonometry). In the right-angled triangle with $A$, $O$ and the top of the building:
$$\begin{aligned} \tan 60^\circ&=\dfrac{69.2}{AO}\\ AO&=\dfrac{69.2}{\tan 60^\circ}\\ &=39.9526\ldots\\ &\approx 40 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
Alternatively, using the 80 m cable as hypotenuse:
$$\begin{aligned} \cos 60^\circ&=\dfrac{AO}{80}\\ AO&=80\cos 60^\circ=40 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
Method 2 (Pythagoras). In the right-angled triangle with $B$ and $O$:
$$\begin{aligned} 72^2&=OB^2+69.2^2\\ OB^2&=395.36\\ OB&=19.9 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
So $AO\approx 20+19.9=39.9\approx 40$ m.

The distance from $A$ to the base of the building is approximately 40 metres.
criteria: Correct answer with all necessary calculations, using Pythagoras' theorem or trigonometry
Progress towards the correct answer with a small error, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Draw a right-angled triangle with opposite side $2$ and adjacent side $3$, since $\tan\theta=\dfrac{2}{3}$.

By Pythagoras' theorem, the hypotenuse is $\sqrt{2^2+3^2}=\sqrt{13}$.
$$\cos\theta=\dfrac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}=\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{13}}$$
Hence the answer is option C.

4789.stem:
A sector of a circle, centre $O$, is shown below.

The points $A$ and $B$ lie on the circle, such that the length of the chord $AB$ is 104 metres, and the length of the arc $AB$ is 126 metres.

The radius is $r$ metres and the angle subtended at the centre by the arc is $2\alpha$ radians.

\exfigure{1316_q24_1}

figures.cap: sector with chord AB 104 m, arc AB 126 m, angle 2alpha at O
solution sketch: right-angled triangle with 52 and angle alpha, hypotenuse r

parts.latex: Show that $\sin\alpha = \dfrac{52\alpha}{63}$.

If $\alpha = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$, find the exact radius of the circle.

Express your answer with a rational denominator.

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{1316_q24_s1}

The perpendicular from $O$ to $AB$ bisects the chord and the angle $2\alpha$. In the right-angled triangle, half the chord is $52$, so
$$\sin\alpha=\dfrac{52}{r}\quad\text{so}\quad r=\dfrac{52}{\sin\alpha}\qquad(1)$$
Arc length $l=r\theta$ with $\theta=2\alpha$:
$$126=2\alpha r\quad\text{so}\quad r=\dfrac{63}{\alpha}\qquad(2)$$
Equating (1) and (2):
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{63}{\alpha}&=\dfrac{52}{\sin\alpha} \\ 63\sin\alpha&=52\alpha \\ \sin\alpha&=\dfrac{52\alpha}{63} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Sets up two equations for $r$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using $r=\dfrac{52}{\sin\alpha}$ with $\alpha=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned} r&=\dfrac{52}{\sin\frac{\pi}{3}} \\ &=52\div\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ &=52\times\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}} \\ &=\dfrac{104}{\sqrt{3}} \\ &=\dfrac{104\sqrt{3}}{3} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ r=\dfrac{104\sqrt{3}}{3}\text{ m}$$
criteria: Finds $r$ correctly using either equation for $r$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find the distance $BC$. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
What is the true bearing of $C$ from $B$? Give your answer correct to the nearest degree.

solutions.latex:
Using the cosine rule in $\triangle ABC$, with $\angle BAC = 50^\circ$, $AC = 12$ and $AB = 9$:
$$\begin{aligned} BC^2 &= 12^2 + 9^2 - 2 \times 12 \times 9\cos 50^\circ \\ &= 86.157\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ BC \approx 9.28 \text{ km}$$

solutions.latex:
Let $\angle ACB = \theta$. Using the sine rule in $\triangle ABC$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{9}{\sin\theta} &= \dfrac{BC}{\sin 50^\circ} \\ \sin\theta &= \dfrac{9\sin 50^\circ}{BC} \\ &= 0.7428\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$$\theta \approx 48^\circ$$
Ambiguous case check: the other angle is $180^\circ - 48^\circ = 132^\circ$, and $132^\circ + 50^\circ > 180^\circ$, so $\theta$ is acute.

Since $C$ is north-west of $B$, the bearing of $C$ from $B$ is
$$360^\circ - 48^\circ = 312^\circ \text{ T}$$
Alternatively, let $\angle ABC = \alpha$:
$$\sin\alpha = \dfrac{12\sin 50^\circ}{BC} = 0.9903\ldots$$
so $\alpha = 82^\circ$, and the bearing is
$$82^\circ + 50^\circ + 180^\circ = 312^\circ \text{ T}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{bearing} = 312^\circ \text{ T}$$
criteria: Finds $\angle ACB$ or $\angle ABC$, or equivalent merit

5348.stem:
A class is on a hike as part of their sports course. They are given the following directions from starting point $A$: They are to walk on a bearing of $062^\circ$ for 14 kilometres to point $B$. Then, they continue on a bearing of $136^\circ$ for 8.5 kilometres to point $C$, before returning to starting point $A$.

\exfigure{1279_q28_1}

figures.cap: triangle ABC with bearings, AB = 14 km, BC = 8.5 km, not to scale

parts.latex: Show that $\angle ABC = 106^\circ$.
Calculate $AC$, the distance that the class needs to travel on the final leg of their hike. Give your answer correct to the nearest kilometre.
Find the bearing that the class needs to take from point $C$ to return to starting point $A$, correct to the nearest degree.

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} \angle ABD &= 62^\circ && (\text{alternate angles, parallel north lines}) \\ \angle CBD &= 180^\circ - 136^\circ = 44^\circ && (\text{co-interior angles}) \\ \angle ABC &= 62^\circ + 44^\circ = 106^\circ \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Source reason for $\angle CBD$ was not given; supplied as co-interior angles. Figure is the question's own.

solutions.latex:
In $\triangle ABC$ use the cosine rule:
$$\begin{aligned} AC^2 &= 14^2 + 8.5^2 - 2 \times 14 \times 8.5\cos 106^\circ \\ AC &\approx 18.27 \\ &\approx 18 \text{ km} \end{aligned}$$

Use the sine rule in $\triangle ABC$:
$$\dfrac{\sin\angle BCA}{14} = \dfrac{\sin 106^\circ}{18.27}$$
So $\angle BCA = 47.437^\circ$ (the obtuse value $132^\circ$ is not possible, since the angles would exceed $180^\circ$).

The bearing of $B$ from $C$ is $136^\circ+180^\circ=316^\circ$, which is $46^\circ$ north of west.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Bearing} &= 270 - (47.437 - 46)^\circ \\ &= 268^\circ 33' \\ &\approx 269^\circ \text{T} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds $\angle BCA$ and the $46^\circ$ angle, or equivalent merit
